lesson.title: Finding the Solution by Sight: The Graphing Method
lesson.summary: The graphing method solves a system by drawing each equation's line on the same coordinate plane and reading off the point, if any, where they intersect.
lesson.body:
The graphing method is the most visual way to solve a system of equations. Using the same skills from graphing a single line, plot each equation of the system on the same coordinate plane, either by finding its slope and y-intercept or by plotting a short table of points, and then look for the point where the lines cross. That intersection point, if it exists, is the solution of the system, because it is the only point lying on both lines at once, and it is the same kind of point discussed when solutions of a system were first defined.

This method also gives an instant visual classification of the system. If the two lines cross at a single point, the system is consistent and independent. If the lines are parallel and never touch, the system is inconsistent, with no solution. If the two equations draw as the exact same line, overlapping completely, the system is consistent and dependent. Seeing the picture often reveals which case you are in before any further algebra is needed, which makes graphing a useful first step even when a more precise algebraic method will be used afterward.

Consider the system y = x + 1 and y = -x + 5. The first line has slope 1 and y-intercept 1, so it passes through (0, 1), (1, 2), and (2, 3). The second line has slope -1 and y-intercept 5, so it passes through (0, 5), (1, 4), and (2, 3). Both tables reach the point (2, 3), which is exactly where the two lines cross on the graph. This can be confirmed algebraically since both equations are already solved for y: setting the expressions equal gives x + 1 = -x + 5. Adding x to both sides gives 2x + 1 = 5, then subtracting 1 gives 2x = 4, so x = 2. Substituting back, y = 2 + 1 = 3. Checking the second equation: y = -(2) + 5 = 3, which matches. The solution is (2, 3), and since the two lines have different slopes, 1 and -1, this system is both consistent and independent.

Graphing is intuitive and shows the whole relationship between the two lines at a glance, but it has a real limitation: precision. Reading a graph by eye works well when the solution lands on nice integer coordinates, as it did here, but a solution like (7/3, -1/2) is nearly impossible to pinpoint accurately just by looking at a hand-drawn graph. That limitation is exactly why the substitution and elimination methods, covered next, matter: they produce the exact solution algebraically, with no dependence on how carefully the lines were drawn or how fine the grid lines happen to be.

The plotting and shading skills used here also carry forward directly into graphing systems of inequalities later on, where instead of marking a single intersection point, whole regions of the plane get shaded to represent every solution of the system at once, building directly on the same coordinate-plane habits practiced in this section.
